The analytics-etl ETL job's schedule was changed from 03:00 UTC (off-peak) to 14:00 UTC (peak hours) without approval. It launched at 14:00 and opened 73 long-running analytical queries that held connections for over 40 minutes, exhausting the orders-db connection pool and starving checkout-api and payment-service of connections.

A manually triggered orders-archive batch job started at 14:01 UTC holds row locks on the orders table, causing checkout queries (UPDATE status and SELECT FOR UPDATE) to block on locks for seconds. This dramatically increased query latency (p99 from 40ms to 3s), which held database connections longer and exhausted the HikariCP pool.

A batch job (archiving old orders) started at 14:01 UTC and holds row locks on the orders table. This causes checkout queries (UPDATE and SELECT FOR UPDATE) to block on lock waits, increasing query latency from ~8ms to >1.4s p99. Connections are held 100x longer, exhausting the HikariCP pool (50/50) on all checkout-api instances.

A long-running batch archival UPDATE (pid 48213, started 14:01) holds row locks on the orders table, causing 1-3s lock waits for checkout-api queries. This increased query latency 100x (8ms to 1.4s p50), which increased connection hold time 50x (45ms to 2.3s), exhausting the 50-connection HikariCP pool on all checkout-api instances.

Checkout queries (UPDATE/SELECT FOR UPDATE) began waiting on those locks, average lock wait rose to 1.8s by 14:05, connection hold times increased to 2.3s, and the pool filled to 50/50 on all instances regardless of checkout-api version.

This forced all product-api traffic to the database, increasing query rate 12x and CPU from 22% to 91%, driving latency and 5xx errors. The v5.3.0 deploy worsened impact by shortening TTL (10min→2min) and adding an inventory lookup per request.

final.mechanism: The product-cache primary node was replaced during scheduled host maintenance at 14:03:12 UTC. The replacement started with an empty dataset because persistence is disabled on this cluster, so all 1.9M cached keys were lost. The cache hit rate dropped from 97% to 3% at 14:04, forcing the product API to serve requests from the database directly. This increased database load and latency, causing the 4.2s p99 and 9% 5xx rate. Both API versions are affected because they share the same cache, and the v5.3.0 deploy's shorter TTL (2 min) means more cache churn, which is why its hit rate recovers more slowly (35% vs 58%).

At 14:03:12 UTC the product-cache primary node was replaced during scheduled host maintenance. The replacement started with an empty dataset because persistence is disabled on this cluster, so all 1.9M cached keys were lost. The cache hit rate dropped from 97% to 3%, causing nearly all product lookups to fall through to the database. This flooded the products-db with ~13,800 queries/sec (up from 1,100), driving CPU to 91% and mean query time to 240ms, which in turn caused the product-api p99 latency spike and 5xx errors on both v5.2.9 and v5.3.0 instances starting at 14:04.

A scheduled host maintenance replaced the cache primary node at 14:03:12 with a new node that started with an empty dataset (persistence disabled). This caused a near-total cache miss, which flooded the products database with 12x normal query load and 240ms average query times, producing the latency and 5xx errors on the product API.
